output.summary: Kevin Kelly's essay '1,000 True Fans' (revised version of a 2008 original) addresses the problem that the web's long tail gives creators massive competition and tiny sales, leaving blockbuster stardom as the only apparent route to success. He proposes a middle path: a creator who cultivates roughly a thousand 'true fans', people who will buy anything the creator makes, and who pay directly, can earn a living (about $100 profit per fan per year, roughly $100,000) without needing a hit. He explains why the web makes this newly feasible, how the number adjusts for team size, income per fan and intermediaries, gives examples of fan-funded work (Street Performer Protocol, Watt-Evans, Fundable, Jill Sobule, crowdfunding), and warns that fan cultivation is demanding and not for everyone. The idea matters because it offers creators a more attainable alternative to stardom or poverty.
main_claims: A creator needs only about 1,000 true fans, defined as fans who will buy anything the creator produces, to make a living, not millions of customers.
The math depends on two criteria: earning about $100 profit per true fan per year, and having a direct relationship so the creator keeps the full payment.
The number 1,000 is an order-of-magnitude figure that must be adjusted for income per fan, income needed, team size, media, and the presence of intermediaries who take a cut.

The web makes this path feasible by enabling direct sales and payment, and by the long tail effect, which makes niche audiences findable (any one-in-a-million appeal can find 1,000 fans among billions of people).
True fans also fuel wider income: they surround the creator with regular fans and act as marketing force, and they enable new support models such as micro-patronage, pre-financing and crowdfunding.
The path is an alternative to stardom, not a guarantee: it is time-consuming, not for every temperament, and can be combined with traditional intermediaries.
background: the long tail (distribution of sales across few bestsellers and many obscure items)
what intermediaries such as publishers, labels, studios and retailers do for creators
basic arithmetic and orders of magnitude
crowdfunding platforms such as Kickstarter (a general idea of what they are)

sections.label: core-idea
sections.title: The core idea: a living without millions
key_points: Success as a creator does not require millions of customers; thousands of true fans suffice.
A true fan is defined as someone who will buy anything you produce, such as driving 200 miles to a show or buying every format of a book.
With about a thousand such fans a creator can make a living, though not a fortune.
The essay is an edited 2008 original, revised to drop out-of-date details.

sections.label: the-math
sections.title: How the math works
key_points: Two criteria: earn about $100 profit per true fan per year, and have a direct relationship so you keep the full payment.
1,000 fans times $100 equals $100,000 per year, a living for most people.
One benchmark for support is one day's wages per year per fan.
A thousand is feasible: adding one fan a day takes only a few years, and you could remember the names.
Giving existing fans more is easier than finding new fans.

sections.label: adjusting-the-number
sections.title: Adjusting the number: income, teams, media, and intermediaries
key_points: 1,000 is an order of magnitude, not an absolute: $50 per fan needs 2,000, $200 needs 500, and lower living costs reduce the need.
A duet or team multiplies the fans needed in proportion, linearly rather than exponentially (a 33% larger team needs 33% more fans).
The number may differ by medium (e.g. 500 for a painter, 5,000 for a videomaker) and cannot truly be known except by attempting it; the author admits it may be off by an order of magnitude.
Indirect income, such as ad-supported blogging or publishers taking most revenue, inflates the number of fans needed, but not to blockbuster levels.
Regular fans in concentric circles around true fans may add perhaps 50% to income, and true fans act as marketing force for them.

sections.label: why-now-web
sections.title: Why it works now: direct relationships and the long tail
key_points: Last century's retail model put intermediaries between creators and customers, who often did not even know their customers' names, so creators needed larger audiences.
Peer-to-peer communication and payment on the web let creators sell directly worldwide and keep the full payment, reducing fans needed.
In a peer-to-peer network the most obscure item is one click from the most popular; Chris Anderson named the resulting sales shape the Long Tail.
Aggregators and search engines built recommendation systems that made obscure items less obscure.
A one-in-a-million appeal among billions of people yields thousands of potential fans, so any niche can find 1,000 true fans; the challenge is having them find you.
Big intermediaries are ill suited to serve niches, leaving the tail open to creators.

sections.label: original-problem
sections.title: The original 2008 argument: escaping the long tail
key_points: The long tail benefits aggregators and consumers but is a mixed blessing for creators: it adds competition and downward price pressure without raising their sales much.
Besides a blockbuster, creators can aim for a middle place between the flat tail and the short head: 1,000 true fans.
Creators need to convert lesser fans into true fans via direct contact, and the same processes also nurture lesser fans.
The alternative is often poverty; Ruth Towse's 1995 survey of British artists found average earnings below poverty subsistence levels.
The path is a saner destination: a living instead of a fortune, surrounded by genuine appreciation instead of fad.

sections.label: fan-funding-models
sections.title: Fan-funded models: micro-patronage, pre-financing, and crowdfunding
key_points: Fans help in three ways: buying more per person, spending directly so the creator keeps more, and enabling new support models.
Carl Steadman's microcelebrity idea counted fame to about 1,500 people; related terms are micro-patronage and distributed patronage.
The Street Performer Protocol (Kelsey and Schneier, 1999) has authors announce that they will release a work once donations hit a target, then release it free to everyone.

Lawrence Watt-Evans used a version in 2004 (chapters posted per $100) and gets by on an estimated 200 true fans, supplemented by traditional publishing; game designer Greg Stolze had fifty true fans pre-fund development.
Fundable's all-or-nothing model (Amelia's CD) and Jill Sobule's tiered pledges (raising close to $50,000 of $75,000) show pre-financing in practice.

Today crowdfunding platforms vary (all-or-nothing, partial, Patreon for ongoing work); Kickstarter's successful projects average 241 funders, fewer than 1,000, so a creator with 1,000 true fans can run a campaign, though success depends on what is asked.

sections.label: caveats-and-takeaway
sections.title: Caveats and takeaway
key_points: Cultivating true fans is time-consuming, can become a full-time job, and is not for everyone; creators can hire a helper or manager, which raises the number of fans needed.
Subcontracting fan relations to labels or publishers is possible, but Kelly says they would usually do it worse.
The approach is not exclusive: Kelly himself uses traditional publishers, self-publishing and Kickstarter, and cultivating true fans enriches each route.

Takeaway: 1,000 true fans is an alternative path to stardom, more likely to be reached; Kelly also notes updates, including a disclosure of one artist's finances and a survey presenting a case against the idea, without detailing their content.
